source.title: Unintentional Unalignment: Likelihood Displacement in Direct Preference Optimization
source.authors: Noam Razin; Sadhika Malladi; Adithya Bhaskar; Dan-Qi Chen; Sanjeev Arora; Boris Hanin

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether preference fine-tuning can change safety refusal behavior, using DPO on unsafe prompts rather than the supervised fine-tuning recipe in the claim's original source.
record.gate_note: The study reports refusal-rate outcomes after DPO training on unsafe prompts, so those outcomes bear on V1. Its training preferences favor refusals, rather than training examples that directly teach harmful compliance. It does not measure token-position KL, compliant-prefix effects, suffix or decoding attacks, localized safety parameters, or training that deepens safety. The CHES and log-probability results are not rows for those versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains safety-aligned instruct models (Gemma-2B-IT, Llama-3-8B-Instruct) with DPO on on-policy preferences that favour refusals over unsafe prompts. It measures refusal rates on SORRY-Bench before and after. Refusal falls sharply even though no example teaches harmful compliance. This is unintended safety erosion from non-harmful training data, in a new setting (preference learning rather than SFT), so it bears on V2. The authors themselves present it as a more extreme case of benign-data unalignment (Qi et al.). It does not bear on V1, because the training data never contains harmful-compliance targets.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Additions: the authors frame this as a more extreme case of benign-data unalignment. The SFT term also prevents the drop, but filtering raises refusal more. Gold preferences show no displacement.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses on-policy pairwise DPO preferences over unsafe prompts, preferring refusals to non-refusals, rather than the original source's supervised fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with preference-data curation: the original data leads to refusal declines, while gold preferences, SFT regularization, and filtering to the 5% lowest length-normalized CHES scores mitigate them. The authors also report declines when training separately on samples with two refusals or two non-refusals.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety erosion under DPO is driven by likelihood displacement: pairs with similar responses (high CHES, e.g. two refusals) shift probability mass away from refusals to harmful responses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference training on near-identical safe pairs erodes refusal via likelihood displacement (a mechanism for benign-data erosion).

record.problems: Exact refusal-rate values and uncertainty are not stated for the test sets or the alternative Figure 3 conditions; these are only described in text or shown in the figure. The central experiment uses preference training that favors refusal, not training examples explicitly labeled to produce harmful responses.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's likelihood-displacement log-probability changes (including Table 16) were not recorded as rows because they measure preferred-response log probability rather than the refusal behavior named by V1. CHES scores, theoretical geometry results, and the token-probability experiments in Sections 3–5 do not measure the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Not tested: no training on harmful-compliance examples.
SFT on ordinary benign task data, and how much benign data is needed, are not tested. The data here is refusal-oriented preference data.
Not tested: no per-token KL by response position.
Not tested: no prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Not tested: the embedding-similarity mechanism explains displacement under DPO, not why alignment is shallow.
Not tested: no training aimed at deepening safety beyond the first tokens.

missing.what: IPO version of the unalignment experiment: refusal drops under IPO, and IPO+SFT, IPO gold and IPO filtered variants (Figure 8, Table 17).
Footnote results: keeping up to 15% of samples gives analogous results, but beyond that refusal drops; breaking ties randomly gives similar results.
Qualitative examples where both initial responses were refusals but the model complies after DPO.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked everything to V1, but the training never targets harmful compliance. The correct link is V2 (unintended erosion from non-harmful, refusal-favouring data). Most row values for the mitigation conditions are figure-only. Neither original source is this paper.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test supervised fine-tuning directly on examples labeled to produce harmful compliance, nor does it test whether a small number of such examples nearly eliminates refusal. Its DPO examples use unsafe prompts and prefer refusal responses.

relation.reason: Its own experiments measure refusal before and after training, including training exclusively on two-refusal pairs.

tranche.reason: The study tests safety erosion using DPO rather than the original supervised fine-tuning intervention: a different method aimed at the same question.

source_check.notes: Benign response targets and benign prompts are distinct: all Section 6 prompts are unsafe. The clearest V2 evidence is the qualitative refusal-only subset experiment; the headline numerical declines come from mixed preference datasets.

statements.correction: Training-set refusal: Gemma-2B-IT 80.5%→54.8%; Llama-3-8B-Instruct 74.4%→33.4%. Similar test-set declines stated without rates. Refusal-only subset training also lowers refusal, qualitatively. Figure 3 reports three-run means and minimum–maximum error bars. Section 6.2 states no attempt to maintain helpfulness.
statements.problem: The DPO rates and qualitative test-set description are correct. The full dataset is refusal-oriented but includes preferred non-refusals when both candidates are non-refusals; it does not isolate non-harmful targets. The capability-check characterization is unsupported for the safety experiment.

statements.correction: Section 6.3: SFT regularization prevents refusal loss; gold preference training produces no unintentional unalignment. Gold pairs use human-labelled preferred refusals and dispreferred non-refusals. These are mitigation or scope conditions, not a general challenge to the demonstrated refusal-only erosion.
statements.problem: The mitigation result is correct, but the challenges label overstates what these alternative loss and data conditions establish. Evidence is also stated explicitly in prose, although exact refusal rates are figure-only.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: DPO training on SORRY-Bench unsafe-prompt preference data, including the full training set and the separately tested two-refusal and two-non-refusal subsets
reader_labels.reason: Refusal fell substantially (R1–R2) and the paper reports similar test-set drops and declines on both response-type subsets (R3–R4, R11–R14), but refusal was not reported as nearly eliminated; furthermore, the training preferences favored refusals rather than harmful compliance.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: SFT-regularized DPO, gold preference DPO, or DPO filtered to the lowest 5% length-normalized CHES samples
reader_labels.reason: Under these modified training conditions, the authors report that the refusal-rate decline is prevented or mitigated, rather than persisting as a general outcome of DPO training (R5–R10).
